title: More LEDs
circuit: 3.3 V -> 330 ohm resistor -> red LED -> ground, 1 to 3 times

expected.math: (3.3 - 2) / 330 = 0.0039 A = 3.9 mA for each LED circuit

mistakes.description: A leg is loose: a row keeps switching between connected and empty
mistakes.hint: One row keeps switching between connected and empty while I measure. That means a leg is loose. Find the row with the yellow light and push that leg in firmly, all the way down.
mistakes.explain: A leg that is not pushed all the way in only touches the metal clip some of the time, so that row keeps connecting and letting go. Push each leg in the yellow row firmly until it stops moving, then check again.

mini_lesson.title: Loose legs make blinking circuits
mini_lesson.idea: A part only works while its metal leg touches the metal clip inside the hole. A loose leg touches, then lets go, then touches again. So the circuit keeps switching on and off, like a lamp with a wobbly cord.
mini_lesson.question: A row keeps switching between connected and empty. What is the most likely reason?
options: A leg is loose in its hole
mini_lesson.why: When a leg wobbles in its hole, it keeps touching and letting go of the clip, so the row comes and goes.

mistakes.description: LED may be backwards, in the wrong row, or missing (the board cannot tell which)
mistakes.hint: Almost no current is flowing, but the row before the LED still has the full 3.3 volts. So the current is stopped at the LED: it may be backwards, in the wrong row, or missing, and the board cannot tell which. Look at the LED's long leg, the one marked + in the drawing: notice which row it is in, and which way it faces.
mistakes.explain: Three things can cause this, and the board cannot tell which one: the LED may be in backwards, it may be in the wrong row (its long leg not in the same row as the resistor), or it may be missing. The long leg (+) should share a row with the resistor, and the short leg (-) should lead to ground.

no_sensor.description: The resistor may be missing, or the LED may be backwards, in the wrong row, or missing (this board cannot measure current, so it cannot tell which)
no_sensor.hint: First look at the LED. If it is very bright or feels warm, pull every wire out of the + line right now: the resistor may be missing. If the LED is dark, the current is stopped at the LED: it may be backwards, in the wrong row, or missing. Look at the LED's long leg, the one marked + in the drawing: which row is it in, and which way does it face?
no_sensor.explain: This board cannot measure current, so four things look the same to it. The 330 ohm resistor may be missing: then the LED gets far too much current and shines very brightly, so pull every wire out of the + line first. Or the LED may be in backwards, it may be in the wrong row (its long leg not in the same row as the resistor), or it may be missing: then it stays dark. The 330 ohm resistor must sit between the + side and the LED's long leg (+), and the short leg (-) should lead to ground.
no_sensor.screen: LED bright or warm?|Pull every wire|out of the + line!

mini_lesson.title: LEDs are one-way doors
mini_lesson.idea: An LED is like a one-way door. Current can only go through it in one direction, and only if the door is connected on both sides. If the door faces the wrong way or is not connected, the current stops.
mini_lesson.question: Current stops right at the LED. What could cause that?
options: The resistor is the wrong color
The LED faces the wrong way, or a leg is not connected
The power is too weak to light it
mini_lesson.why: An LED lets current through only one way, and only when both of its legs are connected.

mistakes.description: No resistor: LED connected straight to 3.3 V
mistakes.hint: The current was far too high, so the power must stay off until it is fixed. What part in the circuit keeps the current small enough for the LED?
mistakes.explain: There was no resistor, so the LED was connected straight to 3.3 volts. Nothing kept the current small, so it shot far past what the LED can handle, and that can burn it out. Put the 330 ohm resistor between 3.3 V and the LED's long leg.

mini_lesson.title: Resistors keep current small
mini_lesson.idea: A resistor slows down electric current, like a narrow pipe slows down water. Without one, a huge amount of current rushes through the LED. Too much current makes parts very hot and can burn them out.
mini_lesson.question: What is the job of the resistor in an LED circuit?
options: It makes the LED change color
It keeps the current small and safe
mini_lesson.why: The resistor limits the current, so the LED gets only as much as it can handle.

mistakes.description: Circuit is not a closed loop (a part is in the wrong row)
mistakes.hint: No current, and no voltage at the LED. Something is not connected. Check that each leg is in the row you think it is.
mistakes.explain: The circuit is not a closed loop. Each part must share a row with the next one: 3.3 V to the resistor, the resistor to the LED's long leg, and the LED's short leg to ground. The lit row is the measuring row, so make sure the resistor and the LED both reach it.

no_sensor.description: Circuit is not a closed loop (a part is in the wrong row), or the LED skips the resistor (this board cannot measure current, so it cannot tell which)
no_sensor.hint: First look at the LED. If it is very bright or feels warm, pull every wire out of the + line right now: its long leg may skip the resistor. If it is dark, something is not connected: nothing reaches the LED's row. Check that each leg is in the row you think it is.
no_sensor.explain: The LED's row has nothing connected, and this board cannot measure current, so two things look the same to it. The LED's long leg may skip the 330 ohm resistor (for example, pushed into the row before it): then the LED gets far too much current and shines very brightly, so pull every wire out of the + line first. Or the circuit is not a closed loop: each part must share a row with the next one, the 330 ohm resistor to the LED's long leg, and the LED's short leg to ground. The lit row is the LED's row, so make sure the resistor and the LED both reach it.
no_sensor.screen: LED bright or warm?|Pull every wire|out of the + line!

mini_lesson.title: Circuits must be closed loops
mini_lesson.idea: Electric current only flows around a complete loop, from the power supply and back again. It is like a train track: if one piece is missing, the train cannot go around. A part in the wrong row is like a missing piece of track.
mini_lesson.question: What does current need in order to flow?
options: A complete loop with no gaps
mini_lesson.why: Current flows only around a closed loop, so one gap stops it everywhere.

mistakes.description: Resistor is bigger than 330 ohm, so the LED is dim
mistakes.hint: The LED is getting much less current than it should, so it is dim. Something is holding the current back more than a 330 ohm resistor would. Look closely at the resistor.
mistakes.explain: The resistor seems to be bigger than 330 ohm, for example 1k (brown-black-red) or 10k (brown-black-orange) instead of 330 (orange-orange-brown). A bigger resistor lets less current through, so the LED is dim. Use the 330 ohm resistor.

mini_lesson.title: Bigger resistor, less current
mini_lesson.idea: A resistor works like a doorway that people have to squeeze through. The narrower the doorway, the fewer people get through each second. A bigger resistor is a narrower doorway, so less current gets through and an LED glows dimmer.
mini_lesson.question: What happens to the current when a circuit has a bigger resistor?
mini_lesson.why: A bigger resistor pushes back harder, so less current flows.

mistakes.description: Current skips the LED (both legs in one row, or a wire around it)
mistakes.hint: Lots of current is flowing, but the LED row has almost 0 volts. The current seems to be going around the LED instead of through it. Look at where the LED's two legs are.
mistakes.explain: The current is skipping the LED. Both LED legs may be in the same row, or a wire may join the two sides of the LED. Each LED leg needs its own row, and nothing else should join those two rows.

mini_lesson.title: Current takes the easy path
mini_lesson.idea: Current always takes the easiest path, like water running downhill. If there is a shortcut around the LED, almost all of the current goes through the shortcut. Then the LED gets almost nothing and stays dark.
mini_lesson.question: Current can go through a light bulb or through a plain wire next to it. Which way does most of it go?
mini_lesson.why: A plain wire is the easiest path, so almost all the current skips the bulb.
